source.title: The Larger They Are, the Harder They Fail: Language Models do not Recognize Identifier Swaps in Python
source.authors: A. Barone; Fazl Barez; Ioannis Konstas; Shay B. Cohen

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether performance changes predictably with model size using a downstream code-generation task and task-specific loss/accuracy, rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on its identifier-swap code task, including model-size trends and chat-model accuracy. It does not test pretraining loss scaling, extrapolation from small runs, compute-optimal allocation, architectural shape, or fitting-choice dependence. Manual prompting examples are qualitative and do not compare scale, so they are not separate scaling rows. Results cited from other papers are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures how task loss and accuracy change with model size on a downstream code task. It reports inverse or flat scaling for most families, which bears directly on V6. It does not measure pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors add that autoregressive text-based models show inverse scaling, while code-trained models scale roughly flat and may turn positive at the largest size, but they do not improve substantially. They conclude that scaling alone does not give this semantic understanding.
record.recipe_differences: Measures likelihood preference or binary-choice accuracy on synthetically constructed identifier-swap code completions, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling trends differ by model family and training regime; the chat-model protocol is binary choice rather than likelihood scoring; the non-builtin swap variant has a smaller loss magnitude.

fits_no_version.finding: Instruction or RLHF fine-tuning at a fixed 175B size worsens task loss relative to base davinci. InstructGPT is also worse than base GPT-3 at each size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-training regime changes downstream inverse-scaling behaviour independently of size.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2023
record.problems: Only a small number of sizes are available per family, and the paper notes some correlation p-values are high. GPT-Codex has only two size points. FLAN-T5 has large error bars. Closed-source API experiments may not be independently reproducible; the Codex models were no longer available. The chat-model protocol differs from the likelihood protocol and parameter counts are unknown.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row cap.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute is not measured.
No power-law fits are extrapolated to larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens.
No variation of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities and no controlled training-regime scaling.
No comparison of fitting methods or parameter-counting conventions.
Predictability from pretraining loss is not tested, and no tasks other than identifier swaps are measured.

missing.what: Per-model classification loss values and standard errors for each family across sizes
Per-model correct, incorrect and invalid percentages for claude-instant, claude, gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4
Which correlations reach p<0.1 (bolded in Table 1); bolding is lost in the text

record.verdict_notes: The task is adversarial by design (an Inverse Scaling Prize entry), so these results bound V6 on atypical tasks rather than typical benchmarks. Footnote 11 frames log-log Pearson as adherence to an inverse power law on task loss, not pretraining loss. The authors note that p-values are high because each family has few sizes.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as compute changes.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests scaling on one atypical Python identifier-swap task; does not establish general downstream predictability or compare performance with pretraining loss.
Does not vary fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, or compute-optimal allocation.
